text: Hypothesis from abstract scan: Apply Q mechanism design framework to analyze incentive compatibility and sandbagging in P Adversarial Review. Assessment: FEASIBLE (Q provides revelation principle, cyclical monotonicity, peer scoring; P provides concrete 3-agent protocol). POTENTIAL GAIN: AR identifies false-consensus failure but does not analyze as strategic problem. Q sandbagging model (capable agents pretending less capable) directly applies to reviewer/critic roles. Non-obvious result: characterize when AR structured disagreement is incentive-compatible vs vulnerable to strategic sandbagging/collusion. Would yield conditions for AR modification or generalization.

Hypothesis evaluation: APPLY Q MECHANISM DESIGN TO AR PROTOCOL. The abstract scan proposal is CONCRETE and SUPPORTED but PARTIALLY OBVIOUS. Q provides revelation principle, cyclical monotonicity, peer scoring for unknown capabilities/alignment. P has 3-agent AR protocol (main/reviewer/critic) with false-consensus failure mode. Connection: Q sandbagging analysis (capable agent pretends less capable) could explain P false-consensus. Q peer scoring could formalize critic-reviewer discipline beyond prompt engineering. LIMITATION: P treats agents as tools not strategic actors; Q assumes agents with preferences. Contribution: Test if AR is incentive-compatible using Q framework; identify sandbagging vulnerabilities where reviewer/critic might strategically underperform; propose mechanism fixes (e.g., peer scoring rules) vs prompt fixes. Feasibility remains ~70 (theoretical analysis). Gain may exceed 50 cap if reveals general principle for agentic tool-design vs mechanism-design tension.

Sharpening the hypothesis: P identifies false-consensus failure mode empirically and fixes via prompt iteration. Q reframes this as incentive compatibility problem. Key insight: false-consensus is not just coordination failure but potential sandbagging equilibrium. Q tools applicable: (1) Revelation principle - can we assume truthful reviewer/critic reports w.l.o.g.? (2) Cyclical monotonicity - does AR allocation rule satisfy implementability conditions? (3) Peer scoring - Q conditions for when critic discipline induces truth-telling. Concrete result path: prove AR violates cyclical monotonicity under [specific capability asymmetry], derive modified AR mechanism that satisfies IC, test empirically. This moves beyond prompt engineering to mechanism redesign.

SHARPENED HYPOTHESIS: P false-consensus is INCENTIVE COMPATIBILITY failure, not just prompting failure. Q revelation principle asks: does AR protocol ensure truthful revelation of reviewer/critic private signals? Current AR: critic audits reviewer, both rewarded for agreement/accuracy. Problem: if critic signals "disagree with low confidence" and reviewer signals "accept with medium confidence", protocol may converge on agreement without evidence grounding. Q insight: need peer scoring where critic reward depends on catching reviewer errors, reviewer reward depends on surviving critic audit. This creates proper incentives for genuine disagreement when warranted. P prompt-fix ("add disagreement explicitly") is fragile behavioral nudge; Q mechanism-fix (peer scoring) is robust incentive structure. Testable: compare AR with prompt-fix vs AR with peer-scoring rewards on SWE-bench.

COUNTERARGUMENT: Agents-as-tools may not have stable preferences required for mechanism design. Q assumes agents with alignment (preferences) and capabilities (feasible actions) that are unknown but exist. P treats agents as LLM calls with prompts - no utility functions, no strategic optimization. If agents lack genuine agency, Q framework is category error. False-consensus may be purely architectural (information flow) not incentive-based. Prompt fixes address information structure; mechanism fixes address incentive structure. Wrong tool for the problem if problem is information not incentives. Response needed: Show that emergent multi-agent behavior in P exhibits quasi-strategic patterns warranting mechanism analysis, or concede hypothesis fails.

NEXT STEPS TO VALIDATE: (1) Formalize AR protocol as mechanism: define agent type spaces (capabilities, private signals), action spaces (accept/reject/revise), outcome rules (when does code get merged). (2) Apply Q revelation principle: construct direct revelation mechanism equivalent to AR; check if truth-telling is equilibrium. (3) Check cyclical monotonicity: can AR implement optimal code quality policy? (4) Design peer scoring variant: critic rewarded for catching reviewer false-positives/negatives; reviewer rewarded for surviving competent critic audit. (5) Predict: peer-scoring AR should reduce false-consensus more robustly than prompt-fix across distribution shifts. If (2) fails (AR not incentive-compatible), hypothesis confirmed. If peer-scoring variant outperforms prompt-fix empirically, strong publication result.

Technical grounding check: Q mechanism design framework has 3 core tools: (1) revelation principle for unknown alignment/capability types, (2) cyclical monotonicity characterization for implementable allocation rules, (3) peer scoring conditions for multi-agent discipline. P AR protocol has 3 roles (main/reviewer/critic) with structured disagreement. P false-consensus failure: agents converge without evidence grounding. P fix: prompt engineering adding explicit disagreement. Q reframe: false-consensus is IC failure where critic lacks incentive to genuinely audit reviewer. Key gap: P does not model agents as strategic actors with private information. Q assumption: agents have preferences over outcomes, can conceal capabilities (sandbagging). Critical question: does P empirical false-consensus match Q sandbagging equilibrium structure, or is it simpler coordination failure? Need to verify if AR protocol has hidden information structure amenable to Q analysis.

Sharpened analysis: P false-consensus on SWE-PRBench suggests reviewer and critic converge prematurely. Q sandbagging model: capable agent pretends less capable to reduce task burden. Mapping: (1) Critic could sandbag by accepting weak reviews (pretends low auditing capability). (2) Reviewer could sandbag by superficial reviews expecting critic won catch errors (pretends low coding capability). Q revelation principle applies if we model reviewer/critic as having private signals about code quality and effort costs. Non-obvious result path: Show AR protocol violates cyclical monotonicity under specific capability asymmetry conditions (e.g., critic capability > reviewer capability but critic reward structure makes auditing costly). Derive modified AR with peer scoring where critic reward = f(catches reviewer errors, not just agreement). This is mechanism redesign, not prompt engineering. Testable prediction: peer-scoring AR should reduce false-consensus on SWE-PRBench more than prompt-fix alone.

GROUND-TRUTH CHECK: Q abstract confirms 3 core tools: (1) revelation principle for unknown alignment/capability types, (2) cyclical monotonicity for implementable policies, (3) peer scoring conditions for multi-agent discipline. Q explicitly models agents with unknown preferences AND capabilities - sandbagging defined as "more capable agent pretends to be less capable". P abstract confirms: AR protocol has 3 roles (main/reviewer/critic), false-consensus failure on SWE-PRBench (agents converge without evidence grounding), fixed via prompt iteration adding "disagreement explicitly". CRITICAL GAP CONFIRMED: P treats agents as tools with prompt-based behavior, NOT as strategic actors with utility functions. P false-consensus is described as behavioral/architectural failure, NOT incentive failure. Q framework assumes agents optimize preferences; P assumes agents follow prompts. Hypothesis validity hinges on whether P agents exhibit quasi-strategic behavior warranting mechanism analysis.
